title: Batch & Cache Runways — Cost Discovery with Pearlline Analytics
summary: High-level discovery focusing on per-token economics, batching and KV/prefix caching strategies, and preliminary pilot constraints. Customer is cost-sensitive with a 6‑month runway for a pilot; seeks guidance on hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs and wants a modeled cost worksheet and an engineering benchmark run.
topics: hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs
next_steps: Avery to send pilot pricing worksheet and unit-econ model
Ravi to propose a short benchmark matrix and required artifacts
Customer to share sample traffic shape (50-200k daily tokens distribution) and a representative prompt set
Schedule a technical deep dive to run a 2k-request benchmark on Redwood Hosted with caching enabled
action_items: Avery Collins (AE): Send pilot pricing worksheet and unit-econ model by 2028-07-18
Ravi Mukherjee (SE): Draft benchmark matrix and list of artifacts to run (sample prompts, expected concurrency, auth tokens) by 2028-07-16
Maya Chen (CTO): Share anonymized traffic histogram and 10 representative prompts by 2028-07-20
Sofia Patel (SRE): Confirm compliance checklist items needed (SOC2/SSO/KMS) by 2028-07-19
transcript:
[00:00:00] Avery Collins (AE): Hi everyone, thanks for joining. We're here to understand Pearlline's constraints and walk through how batching and cache levers affect per-token economics.
[00:00:12] Maya Chen (CTO): Yep hi, thanks. We're trying to figure out if Redwood Hosted gives us the headroom for a six month pilot or if we need to go dedicated — cost is the gating factor.
[00:00:25] Carlos Rivera (ML): I'll add — latency is important for our customer facing summaries, we want 200-300ms p50 for short prompts but can tolerate higher p95s up to 800ms for longer generation.
[00:00:40] Ravi Mukherjee (SE): Good, that's helpful. Two things we typically model: per-token unit price (hosted) and effective token cost after batching + prefix/K V cache. Quick question: how many concurrent users at peak?
[00:00:55] Ethan Wu (Product): Peak concurrency is about 120 simultaneous sessions, average request size is ~300 tokens, but we have bursts up to 1,000 tokens for some analytics flows.
[00:01:08] Lina Gomez (SE): So your token distribution has a long tail. That suggests caching prefixes for short chat-like requests will help a lot — we often see 15-40% cost reduction from prefix cache for chaty workloads.
[00:01:25] Carlos: When you say prefix cache, do you mean full KV cache across requests or something lighter? We've not run a KV cache in production before.
[00:01:36] Ravi: Two options — per-request prefix caching for common prompt beginnings (low friction) and the full KV cache for session continuity which is stronger but requires sticky routing and some memory footprint. We can quantify both.
[00:01:52] Maya: How big is the memory footprint for KV? We're worried about costs slightly shifting to infra costs.
[00:02:00] Ravi: Roughly, KV cache grows with token length and number of active sessions. For 120 concurrent sessions at 1k tokens average, you're looking at tens of GBs of KV state. On Dedicated you'd pay for GPU memory and instance sizing; on Hosted, Redwood manages that and we bake it into the unit economics via optimized batching and multi-tenancy.
[00:02:22] Carlos: Can you give ballpark per-token numbers for hosted vs dedicated? Even rough order-of-magnitude helps.
[00:02:29] Avery: Sure, high level: hosted per-token list price depends on model family — for a medium LLM family we often quote X cents per 1,000 tokens (we'll send exact worksheet), but effective cost often drops 25-60% after batching and cache. Dedicated can have lower marginal per-token cost at high volume but requires a commit and you take on operational overhead.
[00:02:51] Maya: And private/VPC option? Our compliance team prefers data residency and KMS control — we might have to go private for certain clients.
[00:02:59] Ravi: Private gives you network and key control, plus the same runtime. Cost wise private is similar to dedicated but includes an enterprise licensing fee, and there's an ops integration cost up front.
[00:03:12] Sofia (SRE): On SSO and audit logs: we need SAML + SCIM and per-request audit logs forwarded to our SIEM. Is that supported?
[00:03:20] Lina: Yes, we support SAML, SCIM, KMS integrations, and audit log exports. We'll include the SOC2/ICC notes in the security packet.
[00:03:29] Ethan: Back to batching — how aggressive can batching be without violating our latency SLOs? If we batch too long we can blow the 200-300ms target.
[00:03:39] Ravi: Batching is a tunable trade — continuous batching with micro-batches (3–10ms queueing) typically has negligible latency impact. But larger aggregation to improve throughput adds tail latency. We can suggest batching profiles per route.
[00:03:52] Carlos: Do you have any examples where batching alone reduced token cost significantly?
[00:03:57] Avery: Yes — a customer with many small assistant-turns reduced effective per-token spend by ~30% by moving from naive single-request serving to 40–50ms batching windows plus prefix caching. Your workload's long-tail will change that number but it demonstrates the lever.
[00:04:11] Maya: What about quantization? We run open models internally sometimes with int8 and int4 — does Redwood's runtime support quantized model variants?
[00:04:20] Ravi: Absolutely — we support quantized variants where model accuracy tradeoffs are acceptable. That can drop inference cost quite a bit on Dedicated/Private if your workload can tolerate it. For Hosted we may have curated quantized variants depending on the model.
[00:04:34] Carlos: How do fallback policies work if the dedicated pool is maxed? We can't have errors in production flows.
[00:04:41] Lina: We support smart routing and fallback to compatible variants or Hosted with graceful degradation. You can define policies like "route to Dedicated unless utilization > 85% then fallback to Hosted-Lite model".
[00:04:55] Sofia: That fallback sounds useful but raises data residency questions. If fallback goes to hosted, are requests leaving our VPC?
[00:05:03] Ravi: Yes, that depends on configuration. For strict residency you'd configure fallback only to other private equivalents or set no fallbacks; otherwise fallback to hosted is possible but the data plane may traverse Redwood-hosted regions. We'll note options in the worksheet.
[00:05:16] Ethan: Pilot timeline — we need to show finance a model that keeps burn < $X per month for three months. Is there a typical starter pilot you'd recommend?
[00:05:26] Avery: We often recommend a 1–2 week benchmark with mixed prompt shapes, then a 3-month pilot on Hosted with measured batching/cache enabled and a cap on peak concurrency. That gives a good signal for whether to commit to Dedicated.
[00:05:40] Carlos: For the benchmark, what artifacts do you need? We'll prepare sample prompts and a traffic histogram.
[00:05:47] Ravi: The benchmark matrix we propose will include sample prompts, concurrency pattern, success criteria (latency p95, availability), and a traffic histogram. We'll also include a short plan to enable prefix caches and measure hit rates.
[00:05:59] Maya: Are there any hidden costs we should model besides raw per-token charges? Storage of cache, network egress, logging?
[00:06:08] Lina: Good call — consider cache memory (more relevant for dedicated/private), egress if you move responses out of region, and audit/log export storage. We'll make sure the worksheet includes those line items.
[00:06:20] Carlos: Could you demonstrate a small worked example during the technical deep dive? Like show how 30% cache hit + 2x batching improves the effective per-token price?
[00:06:29] Avery: Yep we can run a short live calc and also provide a spreadsheet you can tweak.
[00:06:34] Ethan: Any procurement red flags? We may need a limited term trial contract.
[00:06:39] Avery: We do flexible pilot terms. For Dedicated we'd discuss committed capacity terms; Hosted pilots are usually pay-as-you-go with a pilot credit on sign-up.
[00:06:48] Maya: Ok last thing — legal wants to see encryption in transit + at-rest details and a sample DPA.
[00:06:55] Lina: We'll attach our security and compliance packet.
[00:07:00] Avery: Great. Recap — we'll send the pricing worksheet and pilot model, Ravi will send benchmark matrix, Pearlline shares prompts and histograms, and we'll schedule the technical deep dive for next week. Any other questions?
[00:07:12] Maya: No, that's it. Thank you.
[00:07:15] Carlos: Thanks all.
[00:07:18] (meeting ends)

Notes on transcript quality: occasional names auto-transcribed (KV -> K V, Pearlline spelled variably), filler words left in place to preserve conversational tone.
